description: Our goal is to gain real-world experience using NASA's datasets to solve practical challenges.
summary:
SkyShift is an open-source tool for exploring NASA’s SPHEREx data in your browser. SPHEREx images are enormous, so instead of downloading multi-gigabyte files, SkyShift pulls only the small cutout you care about from the public AWS S3 archive through HTTP range requests. A Rust/WebAssembly and TypeScript pipeline does the processing locally. It aligns repeat observations across SPHEREx’s six detector arrays and 102 near-infrared bands, then co-adds them into calibrated visit stacks. Flip between epochs with the blink comparator, inspect difference images, or play the sky back as a time series.

SPHEREx produces more data than anyone can inspect by eye, so SkyShift adds discovery tools. “Find Movers” flags sources that shift or flare at 5σ, measured against nearby field stars. “Track & Identify” then checks a candidate against Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, and IMCCE SkyBoT. We tested it on the challenge benchmarks: WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis. Spectral previews, RGB composites, and shareable deep-links are built in.

Sky surveys keep growing, but few people can dig into them. With only a web browser, anyone can hunt for brown dwarfs, asteroids, and variable stars. More eyes on the sky means more discoveries.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

SkyShift is a browser-based app for exploring time-series infrared observations from NASA's SPHEREx mission. Citizen scientists and professional astronomers can both use it, and nothing needs to be installed.

  • Streaming only what's needed: A full Level 2 FITS file is about 65 MB. Instead of downloading it, SkyShift sends HTTP Range requests to the public AWS S3 archive (nasa-irsa-spherex) and fetches just the bytes for the pixels you want. A typical field comes to about 0.15 MB, more than 95% less than the full file.
  • Processing in the browser: A Rust engine compiled to WebAssembly runs in background Web Workers, with a TypeScript fallback. It aligns exposures with TAN-SIP WCS reprojection, subtracts the background, and co-adds them into calibrated visit stacks.
  • Viewer and time series: Pan, zoom, read pixel flux values, step through individual exposures, and switch between visit stacks. A blink comparator flips between epochs automatically, and difference imaging (A − B) makes shifting or variable objects stand out.
  • "Find Movers": An automated pipeline looks for sources moving in a straight line across visits at more than 5σ, calibrated against nearby field stars. It also flags brightness changes with forced aperture photometry, and it skips saturated glare and image artifacts.
  • "Track & Identify": Click any source and SkyShift fits its proper motion in arcseconds per year, then cross-matches it against SIMBAD, Gaia DR3, and IMCCE SkyBoT. SkyBoT helps separate solar system asteroids and comets from distant brown dwarfs.
  • Spectral and multi-band tools: Filter across SPHEREx's 102 near-infrared channels, pull quick-look spectra, build 3-color RGB composites across detector arrays, run comparison-star differential photometry, and decode instrument contamination flags.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Easy to start: No DS9, IRAF, or Python/Astropy, and no local install. It runs in any standard desktop or mobile browser.
  • Fast and light on bandwidth: Reading slices of the raw FITS data straight from the cloud keeps loading quick, even on a modest connection.
  • Good signal-to-noise without losing time resolution: SPHEREx revisits a patch of sky every six months, with about 20 exposures per band at different wavelengths. Co-adding within each visit brings out faint targets like WISE 0855, which is invisible in single frames, as clear 8–12σ detections. The motion between visits stays intact.
  • Open and embeddable: Deep links (?ra=...&dec=...&fov=...&mark=... and embed=1) make it simple for educators, researchers, and citizen science portals like Backyard Worlds to put live SPHEREx views in forums, blogs, and papers.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 infrared bands every six months, producing data on over a billion objects. That is more than automated pipelines can handle alone.

SkyShift opens this data to volunteers, students, and astronomers around the world so they can search it together. We want to speed up real discoveries: ultra-cool brown dwarfs, undiscovered near-Earth asteroids and Kuiper Belt Objects, stellar variability, and supernovae caught before the standard catalog releases.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: TypeScript/JavaScript (ES Modules), Rust (compiled to wasm32-unknown-unknown WebAssembly), HTML5 Canvas, and CSS3.
  • Architecture and web APIs: Web Workers for multi-threaded reprojection and stacking, IndexedDB for client-side metadata and tile caching, and the Fetch API with HTTP Range requests.
  • Backend and DevOps: A lightweight Node.js proxy for non-CORS SIA2/TAP queries and CDS Sesame name resolution, Docker/Podman containers, GitHub Actions CI/CD for automated testing and container builds, and Azure Container Apps.
  • Archives and APIs: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (SPHEREx DR1/QR3 collections and the AWS S3 mirror), CDS Sesame and SIMBAD for name resolution and object classification, ESA Gaia DR3 for proper motion and astrometry, and IMCCE SkyBoT for solar system ephemerides.
  • Hardware: Ordinary development machines. The app itself runs client-side on regular laptops, tablets, and smartphones.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Cloud-native computing for astrophysics: Most web tools either lean on heavy server-side rendering or make users download huge raw datasets. SkyShift uses HTTP range requests and in-browser WebAssembly to do the stacking, reprojection, and photometry entirely on the user's device, in milliseconds.
  • A new take on the blink comparator: Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930 with a mechanical blink comparator. SkyShift brings that method up to date by pairing human pattern recognition with statistical motion analysis, local astrometric calibration, and cross-catalog lookups in one interface.
  • Taming 102 bands: Rather than throwing 102 separate image channels at the user, SkyShift groups the data into visits across the six physical detector arrays. Users can switch between broad visit stacks for the best sensitivity, 3-band RGB false-color composites, and narrow-channel spectral extraction.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • S3 and CORS: IRSA's TAP and cutout services send no CORS headers for browsers and return bulky 4 MB files per cutout. We built around the public AWS S3 mirror, which supports direct and secure range queries from the browser.
  • Epoch-aware coordinates and proper motion: High proper motion targets such as Barnard's Star, which has moved 4.5 arcminutes since J2000, sit far from their catalog coordinates. We propagate proper motion so the viewer centers on where the object was when SPHEREx observed it.
  • False positives and glare: Cosmic rays, diffraction spikes, and detector saturation all create false signals. "Find Movers" requires a linear path of at least 5σ across multiple visits, calibrates registration offsets against real field stars, and masks saturated cores so blooming glare is not reported as a moving object.
  • Scientific integrity: SPHEREx visits sample different wavelengths across a band, so simple frame subtraction can produce fake variability. We added wavelength matching, differential comparison-star analysis, and inspection of instrument FLAGS so users can see where a detection came from and how far to trust it.
